entries.title: D.C. Groups Hit the Road to Flip Congress — And Gain Statehood
entries.summary: A new message promotes D.C. statehood as a tool to fight the Republican agenda nationwide.
entries.content:
A new coalition of D.C. groups and activists has a message for Republican members of Congress: If you mess with us here, we’ll mess with you on your home turf.

The coalition — known as Defend D.C. — says it will spearhead and supercharge efforts to send city residents into surrounding states ahead of the November midterm elections, with the purpose of supporting Democratic challengers and help flip at least the House of Representatives, if not also the Senate.

Proponents say the push to influence the outcome of the elections stems from the reality that D.C. — a federal district with no voting representation on Capitol Hill — is often at the mercy of Congress, and that the Republican majority that has controlled it over the past 20 months has more aggressively interfered with the city’s local affairs.

“Congress has used its power over D.C. to attack us. So Washingtonians are banding together to use our collective power to change Congress,” said Robert White, an at-large D.C. Council member who is also the Democratic nominee for the District’s nonvoting delegate to Congress, at a news conference Monday. “We are going to where the votes are. When politicians somewhere else believe they can come into our city and take away our rights without consequences, then we will go into their communities.”

White and other organizers say the initial focus will be on competitive congressional districts within driving distance of D.C., largely in Virginia, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. While they did not identify every candidate they will target, on Monday they singled one out: Rep. John McGuire (R-Virginia).

“For generations politicians have assumed that there will be no consequences for attacking D.C., that because we don’t have a vote we can’t threaten their power. Well, that changes today. Today we are here to say, ‘John, when you choose to attack D.C. instead of serving your residents, then you’re going to have to deal with all of us,’” said Greg Jackson from Free D.C., a local protest group that grew in the wake of President Donald Trump’s decision in August 2025 to deploy the National Guard in the city.

McGuire — whose district encompasses a swath of central Virginia including Charlottesville and Lynchburg — was the author of a bill that passed the House in March that would permanently codify Trump’s efforts to assert control over D.C. He is being challenged by Tom Perriello, who represented the district from 2009 to 2011. The Cook Political Report has described the seat as “fairly safe” for McGuire to hold.

D.C. residents traveling near and far to canvas for their preferred congressional and presidential candidates isn’t new, and played a significant role in the city’s success in pressuring Congress to grant it an elected mayor and council more than 50 years ago. In the early 1970s, D.C. residents with roots in South Carolina travelled there to help organize against Rep. John McMillan, a longtime foe of the city’s push to gain more autonomy from Congress. In 1972, he lost, in large part because of Black voters.

Defend D.C. and other groups have adopted a subtle yet significant shift in their messaging that they believe could be more successful for them: Selling D.C. statehood as a raw political tool to get two more Democratic senators and push back against the Republican agenda.

“We’re no longer talking about D.C. statehood because it’s the right thing to do. It remains the right thing to do,” White said. “But D.C. statehood is a national response to redistricting and the gutting of the Voting Rights Act, which is something everyone in this nation understands.”

In the past, advocates for statehood — which passed the House of Representatives twice at the start of the decade, but stalled in the Senate — carefully spoke of the cause as one of democratic principles and fairness. Republicans, including Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) and even Trump, derided it as a means by Democrats to get two more senators. Now, White and others agree that the push for statehood boils down to political power.

“I have studied history to understand how and why some states became states,” he told NOTUS. “The Dakotas didn’t become two states just because. They became two states because they said, ‘Why take two senators when we can have four?’ Well, we deserve two senators. We’re not trying to get extra, just what we deserve.”

The shift in messaging is backed by Amy Vruno, the executive director of D.C. Vote, a long-standing organization that has advocated for and educated people on D.C. statehood and autonomy.

“Many of the things we’re engaging people around is, ‘What is an issue you care about and how could D.C., if it has representation and two votes in the Senate, be in alliance with you?’” she said. “Some people care about health care, some about climate, some about reproductive rights. There are many issues that might motivate someone in their home turf that D.C. residents would be in alliance with.”

entries.title: What $1.5 Million Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia (Back-to-School Edition)
entries.summary: Our column compares home listings across the DMV.
entries.content:
Most D.C.-area public school students head back to classrooms this week, and as parents struggle to get their children out the door with the correct backpacks, lunches and sneakers, they may be thinking: Wouldn’t it be great if the kids could just walk to school? No more missing the bus because someone forgot their tablet.

For our back-to-school real estate column, we compared three homes that are walking distance from in-demand public elementary schools.

Realtors we spoke with shared an important tip: Don’t ask your agent to provide advice on specific schools; such recommendations may run afoul of fair housing laws. Do your own homework. Once you have a few schools in mind, approach agents with ideas for areas and neighborhoods.

School reputations reliably drive up home values for single-family homes across the DMV. In the District, the most in-demand schools are in the upper Northwest and Capitol Hill neighborhoods. In Virginia, some pricey neighborhoods don’t necessarily have the highest-performing schools. In Maryland, schools with the highest test scores are clustered in the southwest corner of Montgomery County.

Have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming D or M or V column? Let us know at metro@notus.com.

D.C.

Untitled
The listing: 131 11th Street NE, Unit PH

The price: $1,499,000

The specifics: Sitting atop a newly remodeled Victorian row home remodeled into three condos, this four-bedroom unit has plenty of room for kids, while coming in at a slightly lower price point than some single-family homes in the neighborhood. A giant kitchen island makes it easy to eat breakfast and assemble lunch boxes. A con is there’s a deck and patio but no substantive backyard; a pro is the home is two blocks from the green expanse of Lincoln Park.

The school: Forgotten-lunch-box runs don’t get easier than this. Maury Elementary is less than four blocks away, a neighborhood school that consistently ranks among the District’s top 10 schools for reading and math scores and has a 15:1 student teacher ratio. Sotheby’s real estate adviser Mattia D’Affuso says there are a handful of kid-friendly homes in the neighborhood, but it’s not easy, and many cost more than this. “There is considerable competition for homes that combine a desirable school boundary with enough space for a growing family, a convenient location and move-in-ready condition,” he said.

Sell us on it: This 11th Street listing “offers a combination that can be difficult to find at this price point in D.C.: nearly 3,000 square feet, four bedrooms, parking, outdoor space and a high-quality renovation, all within the Maury Elementary boundary,” D’Affuso said.

Maryland

Untitled
The listing: 11809 Becket Street, Potomac

The price: $1,595,000

The specifics: This Georgian colonial in the Roberts Glen neighborhood was built in 1971 but renovated with a two-story addition and an enormous deck. With four bathrooms to match the four bedrooms, no one should be fighting over sinks in the morning. A mudroom “drop zone” is perfect for storing sports equipment and backpacks. After school, kids can play in the cul de sac, the half-acre yard or the basement rec room.

The school: We don’t know if there are any “sideways stories” straight out of the children’s book series, but there is definitely a Wayside Elementary in Montgomery County, and it’s only half a mile from this Becket Street house. U.S. News & World Report ranked Wayside in its top 15 schools for the state. Single-family detached homes within the Wayside boundary can range from roughly $900,000 to $2.5 million, or $3 million, occasionally, says Meg Percesepe, a sales agent with Washington Fine Properties.

Sell us on it: Citing the “hardwood flooring, recessed and designer lighting, and custom millwork throughout,” the listing calls this “a truly turnkey property.”

Virginia

Untitled
The listing: 3831 N Vernon Street, Arlington

The price: $1,495,000

The specifics: This four-bedroom, split-level home was built in 1972, but many details were updated in the past four years. It’s just over a mile from Chain Bridge, making commutes to the District a freeway-free breeze. The playground at Glebe Road Park, which includes the Gulf Branch Nature Center, is about four blocks away, but there’s also a play set ready to go right outside the door.

The school: Jamestown Elementary, one of Arlington’s best, is half a mile down North Glebe Road. With fewer than 500 students, a 12:1 student-to-teacher ratio and sky-high math scores, U.S. News & World Report ranks Jamestown in Virginia’s top 50 elementary schools.

Sell us on it: “When you walk into this house, you immediately know it’s not just a house, it’s a home,” said Mandy Barnes, an agent with Remax. All the renovations and updates were completed professionally by real people with children, not house flippers, and the family put considerable care into details like new appliances, bathroom fixtures and built-in shelving. And Jamestown Elementary? “That is definitely a selling point,” Barnes said.

entries.title: Republicans Expect Darline Graham to Lose the South Carolina Runoff
entries.summary: Despite a Trump endorsement and big money behind her, the senator is showing signs of struggle as she runs for a full term in her late brother’s seat.
entries.content:
Sen. Darline Graham is facing an uphill climb to win Tuesday’s runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-South Carolina) and secure a full six-year term in her late brother’s seat.

Graham, a political neophyte and the sister of Lindsey Graham, came ahead of Norman and more than a half-dozen candidates in the primary two weeks ago — but there’s a chance that may have been her high-water mark.

According to multiple Republican sources, a Graham victory is viewed as increasingly unlikely, with her debate gaffe last week, in which she said she was “not that informed on national security,” only making matters worse. That she’s now perceived to be in such bad standing is a surprise to many in the party given that President Donald Trump has endorsed her and campaigned on her behalf.

“You’re running a campaign with a virtual unknown that took on all of her brother’s unfavorables without any of the goodwill that her brother has in a very short-sprint special election,” one Republican operative with experience in South Carolina races told NOTUS. Figuring out why she’s in the bad position many Republicans believe her to be in, they added, “isn’t rocket science.”

Public polling has been scant. A Trafalgar Group poll of the race released late Monday showed the two candidates deadlocked at 48% each with a 2.9% margin of error.

A separate survey, obtained by NOTUS, of likely voters late last week and over the weekend from pollsters who support Norman found the lawmaker holding a high-single-digit lead over Graham. The lack of public information gathered by neutral pollsters, however, has left many Republicans to go off of vibes.

“Tomorrow’s election is the biggest black box in recent memory here,” said one South Carolina-based Republican operative, who is not involved in the runoff.

Graham, who has only been in the Senate since mid-July, had a very short timeline on which to grieve her brother’s death, learn the ins and outs of the upper chamber and decide to seek a full term.

Despite her famous political last name and Trump’s backing, Graham has encountered a difficult start to life in the spotlight.

While her brother was a powerful presence in the Senate, his popularity and support were not a given in South Carolina. He spent heavily in the lead-up to the June primary to ensure he cleared the 50% benchmark to avoid a runoff because he had drawn the ire of some conservatives who believed his stances were out of touch.

As his popularity started to flag, it became even less likely that his star power in conservative circles would translate to his sister.

“Her only good is hyper-engaged Trump voters. There is no Darline Graham voter,” the Republican operative who’s worked on South Carolina races said. “No one’s voting for Darline because of Darline.”

Graham’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Graham also lacks a record, which has left voters and other Republicans confused about where she stands on most issues. She’s attempted to appeal to Republicans by co-sponsoring a number of measures, including anti-abortion legislation and the SAVE America Act, the voting-restriction legislation that is a priority for Trump and many conservatives.

Her lack of policy chops showed up in a big way on Tuesday, when she flubbed a question about whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the U.S. She told debate moderator Greta Van Susteren that she is “not that informed on national security.”

“But I do support the military,” she said after pausing for a few seconds. “I’m not a polished politician. National security is not my thing.”

That response has gotten a chilly reception from many in the party who believe the exchange only emphasized her lack of experience. The South Carolina-based Republican operative said that the low-propensity voters she did well with in the primary, many of whom were driven by Trump’s endorsement and favorable coverage on Fox News, have fallen off in backing her.

“The trend line has not been good,” the operative said, noting that many of those low-propensity voters are driven in part by day-to-day news. “It’s just not a good headline.”

Some of her colleagues were also taken aback by the remark. When asked what their initial reaction to the debate blunder was, one Senate Republican was curt.

“Fire the debate preppers,” they said, adding that upon Graham’s decision to seek the full term, she should have been studying these sorts of issues. “Anybody with a couple of weeks should have been ready enough for that debate, and there was no evidence of ready in that debate.”

“You don’t have to be an expert,” the member continued. “But you have to have a working knowledge.”

Norman — a staunch conservative who has clashed with his party on spending — has, by contrast, attempted to sell his experience to voters.

“My record is my biggest asset,” he told The New York Times. “I’m a known quantity.”

Beyond her name ID, Graham does have some things going for her. Leading that is the president’s blessing and active support in the final days. He headlined a rally for her in Myrtle Beach on Friday, coupled with a tele-rally on her behalf on Monday night.

Outside groups have also thrown in the lot for Graham. Super PACs and other groups have plowed more than $6 million onto the airwaves to boost her, according to ad data obtained by NOTUS.

Graham also spent Monday campaigning with South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, who threw his support behind her late last week. During a press conference alongside him, she tried to push back on the attacks against her lack of experience

“When people talk about [that] I don’t have any experience, that’s just not true,” Graham said, pointing to her work atop the South Carolina Commission for the Blind and her initial votes after being sworn in. “I feel like I’ve done more … in 20 days than he has done in 20 years.”

As for Norman, his campaign, which he has largely self-funded, has spent more than $1.5 million on ads. Norman also self-funded much of his failed gubernatorial campaign, which only concluded in early June when he finished in third place in the primary.

Operatives noted that Norman is uniquely difficult to run against in a state as red as South Carolina, especially given the structure of a two-week campaign.

“He can always outflank you to the right,” said the Republican operative who’s worked on South Carolina races, pointing to his “likable” personality and that Trump has barely criticized him ahead of Tuesday.

“All of the negatives have already been used against him,” they continued, referring to the governor’s race. “Changing a lot of minds is really challenging.”

entries.title: Putting Up a Fight
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 25, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

It’s time to go on the offensive. 

That’s the message from a new coalition of D.C. groups that will organize residents to travel to congressional districts in neighboring states to support Democratic challengers in their quest to flip the House of Representatives — and maybe even the Senate.

Known as Defend D.C., the initiative stems from the reality that D.C. — a federal district with no voting representation on Capitol Hill — is often at the mercy of Congress, and that the Republican majority that has controlled it over the past 20 months has more aggressively interfered with the city’s local affairs.

“Congress has used its power over D.C. to attack us. So Washingtonians are banding together to use our collective power to change Congress,” Robert White, an At-Large council member and the Democratic nominee for D.C.’s nonvoting delegate to Congress, said Monday at a launch rally.

NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle reports that the effort’s first target is Republican Rep. John McGuire of Virginia’s 5th District, which encompasses a central swath of the commonwealth. But it won’t be easy, as the Cook Political Report has designated the seat as “fairly safe” for McGuire to hold.

Pro-D.C. groups are adapting their message to energize Democrats nationwide, touting the possibility that statehood could bring two more Democratic senators who could help fight the Republican agenda. It’s a big shift from past messaging around statehood, which sought to portray it as a matter of democratic principles and fairness.

“The Dakotas didn’t become two states just because,” White said of the new, overtly political approach to selling statehood. “They became two states because they said, ‘Why take two senators when we can have four?’ Well, we deserve two senators. We’re not trying to get extra, just what we deserve.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

A D.C. high school has been officially renamed after famed Georgetown basketball coach John R. Thompson Jr. Originally known as MacArthur High School, the DCPS school in the Palisades opened in 2023 to help relieve significant overcrowding at Jackson-Reed in Tenleytown. Thompson was a D.C. native, professional basketball player and longtime educator.

Google is combining its D.C. offices under one roof. The company has leased 231,000 square feet of an office building near Union Station, the Washington Business Journal reports.

The Washington Post has been ordered by an independent arbitrator to rehire opinion writer Karen Attiah and provide her back pay. Attiah was abruptly fired last fall, a decision she said was made over comments she posted to social media in the aftermath of Charlie Kirk’s assassination.

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix made for the busiest Sunday on record for the L’Enfant Plaza Metro station with more than 36,000 trips, according to WMATA. The weekend saw a total of 1.15 million bus and rail trips.

D.C. is the U.S.’s second-best city for work, according to a new report by Indeed. The employment website scored cities based on metrics including job opportunity, compensation and work-life flexibility. Greater Boston took first, but D.C. performed particularly well in career mobility — meaning it’s easier to change jobs here and get a raise when you do, according to Indeed.





FROM MARYLAND AND VIRGINIA

ICE arrested more than 1,300 people in Virginia and Maryland during the first two weeks of August in a sweeping operation dubbed “Safe Community — Washington, D.C.,” the Department of Homeland Security announced Monday.

The operator of a Beltsville data center and its former CEO, Deepak Jain, will pay the Securities and Exchange Commission $1.8 million to resolve allegations that AiNET Corp. misled the agency over whether its facility met requirements.





WHAT YOU GET NEAR A GOOD SCHOOL

VA home real estate (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)
Listed for $1,495,000, this four-bedroom, split-level home with a spacious screened-in porch is located just a short walk away from one of the area’s best elementary schools.

Click to guess where this listing is sold:

  1. Maryland
  2. Virginia
  3. D.C.



We’ll let you know tomorrow how many of you got it right.





SPORTS

natty_088 copy.jpg (7997x5334, AR: 1.50)Meet Natty, everyone’s favorite National. NOTUS’ Jesse Dougherty sat down with the 6-month-old lab-retriever mix to discuss life as a team dog. As it turns out, Natty spends most of his days napping, accepting pets from major leaguers, filming promotional videos and training for his future life as a service animal. The team is hosting a six-month birthday party for him tonight as part of its annual “Pups in the Park” event. Happy birthday, Natty!

Training camp update: Monday was supposed to be an off day for the Commanders. But as NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports, Saturday’s lackluster preseason performance against the Lions caused a change in schedule. The team got to work Monday in Ashburn, hoping to shore up any lingering issues with less than three weeks remaining before the start of the season.

The Mystics are headed to the postseason for the first time since 2023. Washington secured its playoff spot late Sunday with a road win over the Portland Fire.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Rockies, 6:45 p.m. (MLB.TV)

WNBA: Mystics at Mercury, 10 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Real estate photo courtesy of Mandy Barnes. Natty photo by Jared Soares for NOTUS. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was A) Thomas Jefferson. He was named chair of D.C.’s first public school board in 1805. A special shout-out to Robert Malesky, who answered first.

entries.title: South Carolina Callin’
entries.content:
Today’s notice: South Carolina on our minds. The speaker’s communism-is-bad-repeat pitch. The Supreme Court doesn’t mail it in. Interior reassigning. And: The Reaganite fan club comes for JD.





THE LATEST

It’s been a topsy-turvy primary season, with ups for anti-establishment candidates, downs for incumbents, patchy polling, an out-of-the-Michigan-blue squeaker and bad Wisconsin bets. Now we turn our attention to one of the few remaining contests: the Senate Republican runoff in South Carolina.

Sen. Darline Graham hopes to hold onto her late brother’s seat with Donald Trump’s endorsement and a last-minute $800,000 cash infusion from MAGA Inc. She won the most votes in the Aug. 11 primary, but gaffes have cleared an opening for an upset by Rep. Ralph Norman. A Trafalgar Group poll of the race released late last night found the two candidates deadlocked at 48% each with a 2.9% margin of error.

Multiple Republican sources told NOTUS’ Al Weaver they think a Graham victory is increasingly unlikely, especially following her debate admission that “national security is not my thing” — not exactly the thing voters were yearning to hear.

“You’re running a campaign with a virtual unknown that took on all of her brother’s unfavorables without any of the good will that her brother has in a very short-sprint special election,” one Republican operative with experience in South Carolina races told NOTUS. “This isn’t rocket science.”

If Norman nabs the Republican nod, it would fit with this year’s prediction-defying theme. There are only a few primaries on the calendar after today — looking at you, Massachusetts — but results from this runoff will be telling.

“There’s just a little tail end of it left,” elections analyzer and Crystal Ball holder Larry Sabato told us of the primary season. “But you never know what could happen. South Carolina will be very interesting.”

Open tabs: Trump Launches Fresh Sanctions Against Iran in Bid to End War (NOTUS); Trump moves to reshape White House’s South Lawn (WaPo); Trump criticism leads to rare criminal charges for Air Force officer (CNN); Administration Prepares to Revoke Up to 200,000 Visas From Asylum Seekers (WSJ); The Tour Guide Who Lived Through 9/11 (NYT)





From the campaign trail


First on NOTUS: The Democratic Governors Association-backed Protect Our Wisconsin is going up with TV and digital ads blasting Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for governor, over data centers, which might be the issue in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, NOTUS’ Christa Dutton tells us. “MAGA Congressman Tom Tiffany sold us out on data centers,” says the narrator in the ad, which the group says is part of a multimillion-dollar ad campaign in the state.

Mike Johnson’s Great American Road Trip: The House speaker is still on the road, crisscrossing through New York and New Jersey, campaigning for a handful of swing seats that could determine who holds the majority in the lower chamber. While Johnson intended to message on the One Big Beautiful Bill tax cuts, NOTUS’ Kadia Goba reports, his delivery often fell to something else: vote Republican to save us from the communists.

After a slew of democratic socialists dominated their primaries in New York City earlier this year, Republicans have pushed hard to cast Democrats as communists, and particularly in those swing districts. As November approaches, Johnson is messaging that hard.

“I can be here all day telling you the reasons we’re going to win but ultimately it boils down to one thing: The Democrat Party is being taken over by communists,” Johnson told a crowd on Long Island.

From the Supreme Court


Go ahead, for now: The Supreme Court allowed Trump to move forward with parts of his executive order restricting mail-in voting ahead of this year’s midterms, NOTUS’ Adora Brown reports.

The court didn’t rule on the legality of the president’s order; rather it declared that states who challenged it could only say they “might” be harmed. “Emphasis on might,” the court said. And it won’t be the final word, as the decision is likely to wind up back in the justices’ hands to deliberate on the overall executive order. “On that score, time will tell,” the per curiam ruling said.

From the Hill


Dad draws a line: At least one House Democrat has left the Congressional Dads Caucus — which is “dedicated to championing the needs of working families” — after the House Ethics Committee opened a sexual misconduct investigation into Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-California), who chairs the group, NOTUS’ Kadia Goba reports.

A spokesperson for Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-Massachusetts) confirmed that he left the caucus following the ethics probe announcement.





THE BIG ONE

Reassignment or resign: The Department of the Interior has reassigned around 30 of its most senior staffers to teams outside of their areas of expertise, sparking concerns over a loss of institutional knowledge, NOTUS’ Eric Katz and Anna Kramer report. The career experts face a tough decision with only two weeks notice: accept the reassignment or resign.

The personnel moves come as the Trump administration is tightening its grip on the top career employees who serve as the liaisons between political appointees and rank-and-file workers.

One employee put it simply: “They want us all to leave and be replaced by more politicals.”





NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

Trump suggested he might militarily attack the bond market. Dana Milbank has thoughts about the options.





NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: D.C. Groups Hit the Road to Flip Congress — And Gain Statehood, by Martin Austermuhle

What $1.5 Million Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia (Back-to-School Edition), by Rebecca Ritzel

Sports desk: Natty and Me: Sitting Down With the Nationals’ Team Dog, by Jesse Dougherty

After a Lackluster Preseason Performance, the Commanders Work Overtime, by Martenzie Johnson





NEW ON NOTUS

It’s no secret that Vice President JD Vance is thinking about 2028. But his comments in recent weeks attacking several conservative icons could potentially alienate old-guard Republican allies if he were to run, NOTUS’ Jeff Stein reports.

Vance has taken shots at various Reaganites in the past few weeks, striking a populist tone. And while any skirmishes are primarily playing out on social media, they provide a look into what the factional rifts may look like come 2028.

“You can’t be the Republican nominee for president if you actually think Margaret Thatcher and Milton Friedman are not the future direction of the party,” said Stephen Moore, a Reagan acolyte who has served as an outside adviser for Trump. “He’s off message right now and that’s going to be a big problem for him.”

Rep. Al Green Wants to Impeach Trump — Again, by Jackie Llanos

Florida Prepares to Roll Back School Vaccine Requirements, by Jenna Monnin

entries.title: J.D. Vance Is Rattling the GOP’s Old Guard
entries.summary: Reaganites see their chance at a comeback in 2028. Vance isn't saying what they want to hear.
entries.content:
Vice President JD Vance has attacked several conservative icons in recent weeks, unnerving many in the Republican Party’s old guard ahead of the 2028 presidential primary.

Last month, Vance criticized British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, an ally of Republican President Ronald Reagan, for economic policies that he said moved the country “further away” from prosperity and Christinianity. Vance said it was “obviously a good thing” that the American right was distancing itself from Milton Friedman, long regarded as the intellectual godfather of modern conservative economics.

And at an event Friday in Ohio, Vance intensified this battle, calling The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board "the voice of big business" that wanted “to ship your jobs overseas” and “let anybody who wants to come into the United States of America with no vetting and no care.”

These broadsides have provoked fresh resistance among the Republican Party’s orthodox economic conservatives, many of whom had long hoped to reassert their free market agenda after the departure of President Donald Trump. Even some Trump supporters now see Vance’s alleged ideological heresies as disqualifying.

“You can’t be the Republican nominee for president if you actually think Margaret Thatcher and Milton Friedman are not the future direction of the party,” said Stephen Moore, a Reagan acolyte who has served as an outside adviser for Trump. “He’s off message right now and that’s going to be a big problem for him.”

It “is very concerning” that Vance was listening to “people who are not Reaganite Republicans and not even Trump Republicans,” Moore said. Vance’s allies dismiss these critics as a narrow elite almost entirely confined to Washington, pointing to the vice president’s high approval rating among Trump supporters.

The skirmishes, primarily playing out on social media, provide an early window into the factional rifts on the right expected to burst to the surface next year once there is an open contest for leadership of the Republican Party.

A spokesman for Vance declined to comment. The vice president’s allies, however, say they relish a confrontation with what several referred to as the “rump” wing of the Republican Party that defied Trump in the 2016 and 2024 presidential primaries.

“The president helped save the Republican Party in large part due to his populist economic message. If he had not come along, the Republican Party would be on the brink of extinction,” said Alex Bruesewitz, a political adviser to the president.

Most polling thus far suggests Vance is highly popular among the president’s supporters, and Trump has faced similar criticisms for his insistence on using tariffs in defense of America’s industrial base.

“The same forces who fought against Trump in 2016, who said he’s an antisemite and a leftist and pro-abortion — all these establishment types are back 10 years later, and now they’re just older, uglier, dumber and with less influence than ever before,” Bruesewitz said.

Vance has broken with conservative economic dogma on a greater scale than Trump, pushing family benefit policies, questioning bedrock assumptions of U.S. monetary policy and suggesting that economic growth has been overrated by policymakers. On Friday, he renewed his attacks on American elites "from both political parties" who "spent the last 40 years telling you it didn't matter if we made things right here or whether we made them in overseas countries," an implicit rebuke to the pre-Trump view of trade on the right.

Phil Kerpen, president of the conservative group American Commitment who described himself as “90%” a supporter of Trump, said Vance has been “clearly trying to be as transgressive against the free market ideological wing of the party as possible as a way to distinguish himself. I think it’s substantively wrong and destructive.”

Already many traditional Reaganites reconciled themselves to supporting or working for Trump despite the president’s support for high tariffs and resistance to cutting entitlement programs like Medicare and Social Security. Vance takes conservative politics further away from the template Reagan set in the 1980s, said Vance Ginn, who served as chief economist in the Office of Management and Budget during Trump’s first term.

“As a classic free-market guy, I’ve been pretty concerned about the direction we’re going down for a while now. With JD Vance, it’s on steroids,” Ginn said. “Yeah, I’m nervous about it. Definitely.”

Vance’s precise policy convictions remain inscrutable on a number of issues, in part because of his relatively short time as a public figure before rising to the vice presidency in which he has marched in lockstep behind the president’s agenda. He has fallen in line behind Trump’s policy positions on taxes, trade, regulation and immigration, leaving his personal positions a matter of some speculation.

When he has taken policy stands of his own, he's shown a desire to break from conservative orthodoxy. Vance has not just been a staunch defender of the president’s high tariffs but gone out of his way to affiliate himself with some of the policy’s most ardent defenders, including Oren Cass, founder of the think tank American Compass.

Where Trump mollified many Reaganite conservatives by passing into law two of the largest tax cuts in modern American history, Vance’s tax positions have been more heterodox.

In 2024, Vance pushed for the elimination of a tax break for large corporate mergers. As a senator, he pushed for a penalty on executives of large failed banks, endorsing legislation with prominent progressive Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts).

Perhaps most strikingly, Vance in 2024 called for the Child Tax Credit to be boosted from $2,000 per child to $5,000. During debates about the tax bill, he also expressed openness to raising the top rate on the richest taxpayers.

As a senator, Vance expressed openness to a $20 minimum wage and called for Google to be broken up. He praised Lina Khan, who was appointed by President Joe Biden to lead the Federal Trade Commission, and who infuriated conservatives by pursuing an aggressive antitrust policy.

In one 2023 clip recirculated among conservatives earlier this month on X, Vance expressed opposition to the dollar’s status as a reserve currency. The world’s banks and governments hold their financial reserves in dollars, which makes it more expensive than other currencies. This depresses domestic manufacturing by making American exports more expensive, but also means that the federal government can run large deficits, which help subsidize consumer lifestyles.

Vance’s call to upend this balance, in place for more than 80 years, has baffled the conservative policy community, though Trump has also expressed ambivalence about the strong dollar policy.

“I am not convinced by his current arguments — trade, monetary policy, getting rid of the reserve currency. All of that is a recipe for things to be very expensive in the U.S., and we have an affordability crisis as it is,” said Doug Holtz-Eakin, who served as a senior policy adviser to Sen. John McCain’s (R-Arizona) 2008 presidential campaign. “This is absolutely being discussed — though one of the beauties of all these discussions is they’re usually way ahead of schedule and totally irrelevant in the end.”

Despite the hand-wringing on the right, Democrats say Vance’s populist instincts are largely for show.

The vice president has long been close with billionaires in Silicon Valley. Vance ultimately supported Trump’s 2025 tax bill, which the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimates will result in 10 million people losing their health insurance. The legislation, the largest safety net cut in modern American history, also slashed food stamps for lower-income households.

“Vance may try to distance himself from neoclassical economics on his press tours, but I don’t think we’ve ever seen any action from him that’s any different,” said Liz Pancotti, vice president of policy, advocacy and research at the Groundwork Collaborative, a left-leaning think tank. “He talks a big game, but falls to the exact same corporate interests that the party is beholden to.”

On the other side, some conservatives are also holding out hope that the Republican Party turns on Trump’s policies, whether in the 2028 primaries or sooner.

Most Republican members of Congress, as well as most Republican governors, remain more aligned with Reagan economic principles than either Trump or Vance. It is also possible that a disastrous 2026 midterm outcome for the Republican Party, caused in part by high prices, would intensify internal criticism of the president’s tariff policies.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), a potential 2028 contender, has already broken with the president’s trade agenda. Former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, another potential presidential candidate, is similarly widely viewed as articulating a more business-friendly agenda than Trump or Vance.

“I don’t think you’re going to see people attack Trump, but you could see people really sharply break with his policies,” said Michael Strain, an economist at the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank, who has been critical of the president’s economic policies on trade and spending.

The Republican base might not be interested in going back to the traditional conservative views, though. Voters without a college degree comprise a far higher share of the Republican Party under Trump than they did several decades ago, and it is unclear whether they would support a candidate who bucks Trump’s economic views.

“The incipient ‘Never Vance’ campaign is a precise rehashing of ‘Never Trump’ from 2016,” Michael Knowles, a conservative political commentator, said. “It seems to me a small group, albeit one with outside visibility since it’s clustered in the Beltway. All of which is probably good for the vice president if he does indeed run in 2028, as it more firmly establishes him as the authentic successor to Trump.”
entries.author: Jeff Stein

entries.title: ‘They Want Us All To Leave’: Interior Reassigns Dozens of Senior Staff
entries.summary: Around 30 top staffers have been reshuffled, with some people moving to teams outside their areas of expertise.
entries.content:
The Interior Department has reassigned around 30 of its most senior staffers to teams largely outside their areas of expertise, alarming lawmakers and federal government workers already worried about the Trump administration’s erosion of institutional knowledge at the agency.

The reassignments mirror an approach President Donald Trump employed in his first term, when the Interior Department, under then-Secretary Ryan Zinke, suddenly shifted around dozens of career Senior Executive Service personnel. The move was met with widespread condemnation from congressional Democrats and led to whistleblower complaints and lawsuits, which accused the administration of sidelining key staff working on climate change and other issues it disfavored.

A subsequent inspector general report faulted Interior for allowing political appointees to exclusively determine the assignments and for failing to justify the moves.

This time, Interior, helmed by Secretary Doug Burgum, has shifted some of its most senior, longest-serving career staffers from the Fish and Wildlife Service, U.S. Geological Survey, Bureau of Land Management, central agency headquarters and some smaller offices, according to a dozen current and former employees familiar with the moves. The employees were given two weeks to decide if they would accept the role or resign from government.

The personnel moves follow new policies that have tightened the administration's grip on the Senior Executive Service staff — the top career employees in federal government who serve as a direct liaison between political appointees and rank-and-file workers — to ensure they fully adhere to the president’s policies.

One of the people reassigned to a different bureau within the Interior Department described the reassignments broadly as “punitive.”

“They want us all to leave and be replaced by more politicals,” this person said.

Before the shake-up, Interior had already shed around 40% of its senior executive cadre since Trump took office, largely through deferred resignation and deferred retirement programs intended to shrink the agency.

The reassignments, described by one 20-year veteran of Interior as “highly unusual,” represent at least 20% of the most senior career employees who still remain at the agency. The actual percentage could be far higher, because some of these executives have agreed to step down at the end of September.

In a statement, the Interior Department said it would not comment on individual personnel matters, but called reassignments “a routine management tool used across administrations.”

“The Department continues to align senior leadership and resources to best support its mission, improve organizational effectiveness and deliver results for the American people,” a spokesperson for the agency said.

Employees said the reshuffling of top staff would lead to a loss of expertise. While these management positions were designed to lead any team and therefore be moved around, many of those impacted by the recent moves had spent their entire careers in one office because of their technical knowledge in that area.

Cynthia Martinez, until this week the longtime director of the National Wildlife Refuge System, had worked for the Fish and Wildlife Service since 1993 and the Refuge System since 2010. Her educational background is focused on biology, fisheries and wildlife science.

She has been reassigned to the USGS Natural Hazards Mission Area, which monitors natural hazards and natural disasters, according to multiple people familiar with the change.

“She has spent her whole career in refuges,” one USGS employee said. “She knows nothing about volcano or earthquake science.”

FWS also reassigned Jerome Ford, who led the related Migratory Birds program since 2011. Funding for the lands that make up the National Wildlife Refuge System largely comes from fundraising by the Migratory Birds program, and now both organizations have lost the civil servants who led them for more than a decade.

David Applegate, who served as USGS director in the Biden administration and was most recently its chief scientist and head of the Natural Hazards office, is moving to Interior headquarters. One source briefed on the overall reassignment effort said moves like that one “don’t make sense,” and that the administration may be trying to curb his influence.

“I think they’re just trying to send a message,” the source said. “If you don’t get in line, maybe this is what’s going to happen.”

Martinez, Ford and Applegate did not respond to requests for comment.

“Shuffling seasoned scientists and land management professionals around into roles outside their areas of expertise means Americans can’t get what they need from our lands agencies, including timely permits for projects, protection from wildfire, and science-based management of our lands and waters,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, the top Democrat on the Senate’s Energy and Natural Resources Committee. “The American people deserve better than this.”

As Interior has instituted more political oversight of all department operations, employees expressed concern that executives who helped win political appointee support for key programs would now be sidelined.

“Agencies have in good faith been justifying everything to the nth degree with hope of approval and continuation of their good work,” another USGS employee said. “Upending the remaining executive leadership means starting all over, reeducating new leaders, which means further delays of partnerships and good work.”

A senior FWS employee said senior executives develop institutional knowledge that help offices function through relationships both inside and outside government.

“They have relationships with people throughout the organization in a way that makes things tick, and have relationships with state and local government, tribal government, NGOs, and other key partners that have a stake in the organization's mission,” the employee said.

Ray Limon, who served as deputy human resources director at Interior during the mass reassignments in Trump’s first term, called that era a “crazy time” when midnight emails alerted staff of their new roles. Limon subsequently became the top HR official for the department and, with then-Secretary David Bernhardt’s backing, helped institute new rules to provide more structure for that process.

“It felt like people were just being moved around without identification of where new work needed to go,” Limon said of the 2017 reassignments, noting he was not directly involved in that decision-making process. “Absent information of why people were being moved, that information gap will typically lead to confusion and not generate, necessarily, a lot of good will. There wasn’t necessarily a logic or a pattern to which individuals got reassigned and which didn’t.”

Limon’s process was meant to give executives 30 days’ notice for an intra-agency move within the same geographic area, or 90 days if it was to a new agency in a new location. It also allowed the employees to ask questions and push back.

It does not appear that Interior followed that process for this month’s reassignments.
entries.author: Eric Katz, Anna Kramer

entries.title: Natty and Me: Sitting Down With the Nationals’ Team Dog
entries.summary: Meet the team's youngest and sleepiest star.
entries.content:
I was 15 minutes into the interview when I realized a slight problem: My subject was asleep. Like, snoring asleep. A not-waking-up-till-the-TV-goes-off kind of sleep. Dead to the world.

But, being a professional and all, I kept asking questions. I asked how he got his name. I asked for the latest skill he’s learned. I asked about the attention, the cameras, the nonstop pulls on his schedule. And it was a good thing I didn’t need him to answer any of this. Natty, the Nationals’ team dog, has people for that.

"He had a long photo shoot today," Jackie Cheshire, one of Natty’s two handlers, told me. "This is his nap.”

It’s not easy work, you know, accepting all these pets, being such a good boy all the time. In his first season with the Nationals, Natty, a 6-month-old lab-retriever mix, has been everywhere. He was in a video with James Wood pandering for All-Star votes. He has made many appearances at Nationals Park, where he’ll trot around the clubhouse, then the field, then wherever the hell he wants, often posing with a player or five. He was even featured by WeRateDogs on X. (Hello, 9.1 million followers, here is my very long tongue and an adorable photo of me sleeping with a baseball glove as my pillow.) The account rated Natty a 13 out of 10.

Smart marketing by the Nationals. Dogged, even. (Sorry, sorry.) On Tuesday, the team is throwing Natty a birthday party, which could be a decent way to get some people to a Nats-Rockies game in late August. There will be a combine for dogs, including a “showcase of obedience on the pitcher’s mound,” according to the press release. There will also be, as ever, a lot of people looking for Natty, which has doubled as an important part of his training this summer. Natty is in the process of becoming a service dog with an organization called Canine Companions.

“He's had to learn that when he's at the park, the rules are a little bit different for him,” Cheshire explained, petting Natty while he kept snoozing in her lap. Natty splits his time between Cheshire and Laura Toelle, who joined the interview. It was Natty’s first ever Zoom call. I also hope, for his sake, that it was his last.
natty_335 copy.jpg (8192x5462, AR: 1.50)“We always let the puppies engage with people because we want them to be well-socialized and meet people of different races and different abilities and not be afraid,” Cheshire continued. “But then at some point of raising them, we start telling people: ‘No, you can't pet them when they're out in public, because we don't want them to seek out being pet.’ Service dogs are supposed to be focused on their person and not distracted by every person out in the community.”

A little inside baseball on covering the sport: If I want to interview a player — like, say, James Wood — there’s an allotted time for reporters to be in the clubhouse before each game. I will typically hover near his locker, wait for him to pop into the room, then ask if he has a few minutes, which is never really a few minutes (which he knows because he’s a pro at this, among other things). If he has the time, we chat. If he doesn’t, we’ll plan to later. Simple, done.

Now if I want to ask manager Blake Butera a question, he has two press conferences a day, one before each game, one after. If I want to catch someone in the front office, the best bet is to hang around the dugout during batting practice. But if I want to write about Natty? When I asked a member of the PR staff in June, she responded, straight-faced, that “I’m not actually in charge of his schedule, someone in corporate partnerships is, but he’s had so much media that whenever I see his handlers, I tell them we have this, this, this and this.” I noted that Natty seems to have a lot of handlers.

“Oh, God,” she responded. “So many.”

Eventually, I squeezed my way onto Natty’s schedule. We talked. He mostly slept. And later, when we were setting up photos, the PR staffer noted that timing could change because of Natty’s breaks to rest or go potty. This pup, he’s just like us.
natty_106 copy.jpg (7871x5247, AR: 1.50)natty_374 copy.jpg (8082x5388, AR: 1.50)“We are always training,” Toelle said. “Everything is a training opportunity. Even if he’s just sitting with us at a coffee shop, that's training. It may not look like training, but he's absolutely gaining skills that will benefit him when he goes on to become a service dog.”

As for those questions I mentioned earlier, Toelle and Cheshire helped fill in the gaps. The Nationals worked with Canine Companions to name Natty, though there are rules when it comes to naming service dogs. Two hard syllables are preferred, Cheshire told me, especially since they don’t know what kind of disability Natty’s eventual owner will have. These parameters pushed “James Woof” out of the running.

As for Natty’s latest skills, they were still hammering the basics, such as sit, down and stand, when we spoke earlier this summer. But the goal is for Toelle and Cheshire to teach Natty about 35 cues before they pass him off to professional trainers next August. With Toelle and Cheshire, a high-level cue will have him stand on his hind legs while pressing his front paws on a wall. That will set up the professional trainers to teach Natty how to operate light switches or press a button for electric handicap doors.

“I like to say that we teach him basic math and they teach him algebra,” Cheshire said. “We give him that foundation that they can build on.”
natty_078 copy.jpg (7516x5011, AR: 1.50)Which brings us to the bittersweet part of Natty’s setup with the Nats. After spending his first 18 months with Cheshire and Toelle, Natty will do a half-year with the pro trainers on Long Island, then set off for life as a full-time service dog. In recent years, there’s been a lot of talk, much of it warranted, about the Nationals not keeping their stars around long term. But in this one case, the team will actually have no choice, raising questions about whether they might look to trade Natty for prospects over the winter.

(Pause for effect.)

(Pause a little longer to consider writing a better joke.)

Just kidding, of course! He’s not going anywhere quite yet.
entries.author: Jesse Dougherty

entries.title: Billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller’s WSJ Op-Ed Criticizing Bessent Was Written With AI
entries.summary: “I write everything using AI now,” Druckenmiller, who questioned the treasury secretary’s bond market interventions, said.
entries.content:
A billionaire acknowledged on Tuesday that his widely read opinion column in The Wall Street Journal criticizing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s bond market intervention was written using artificial intelligence.

Stanley Druckenmiller, a former hedge fund manager who founded Duquesne Capital, published “Let the Bond Market Speak” on Monday, questioning Bessent’s interventions to hold down yields on U.S. treasuries. The article drew added attention because Druckenmiller worked with Bessent under George Soros, and is sometimes described as a “mentor” to the treasury secretary.

Pangram, an AI detection tool, found that Druckenmiller’s op-ed had been written using artificial intelligence, according to multiple social media posts. In an interview with NOTUS, Druckenmiller said “of course I used AI” when writing the column, and argued he didn’t see a problem with doing so.

"There's a reason I moved from an English major to being an economics major," Druckenmiller said. "I'm not embarrassed by it … I write everything using AI now for the same reason I use a calculator when I do math problems.”

A spokesperson for The Wall Street Journal did not immediately return a request for comment.

The use of AI by economists and other experts in writing opinion pieces has gained renewed scrutiny as the tool has become more widely used.

Earlier this month, Harvard professor Ricardo Hausmann published a column in the Financial Times about Trump's tariff regime. The column appeared laced with AI-inflected language, and the Financial Times later appended a note saying: "It has come to our attention that AI was used to condense a longer draft of this column prior to submission to the FT and our own editorial involvement. The FT editorial code of conduct specifically prohibits the use of AI in the writing process."

Druckenmiller’s op-ed also included numerous phrases that sound like writing generated by AI, including: “There is a quieter cost, too” and “This wasn’t liquidity management, it was price management.”

A Pangram test posted on social media by the economist Claudia Sahm found that "100 percent of this text is AI.” Druckenmiller denied that “the whole thing” was written with AI and said that he rejected many of the AI’s suggestions during the writing process.

Some media experts have expressed concern about the proliferation of the tool. Chris Roberts, an associate professor at the University of Alabama specializing in journalism ethics, said “using AI raises questions about how much time and thought actually went into the piece.”

“We see a ton of this. We’re going to see more of this,” Roberts said. “Any time you take humans out of the process of communicating to other humans there can be blowback when the words or the intent is wrong, or it doesn’t sound like a human.”

Druckenmiller dismissed the use of the tool as unimportant because the op-ed reflected his intended meaning.

“I don’t know why this is relevant,” Druckenmiller said. “My name is on the piece. It’s my message.”
entries.author: Jeff Stein

entries.title: Trump Threatens to Rename Lake Ontario ‘Lake America’ as Trade War Escalates
entries.summary: Trump said the United States didn’t expect to be “doing much business with Ontario any longer.”
entries.content:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday threatened to rename Lake Ontario, the body of water between Canada and New York, “Lake America” after collapsed negotiations over the weekend sparked an escalating trade war between the two historic allies.

Trump, in a post to Truth Social, said Tuesday that the name change was under “serious consideration” because the United States didn’t expect to be “doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

The Trump administration and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney began sparring late Friday night over who was to blame for the failed talks, which triggered a 50% U.S. tariff on some Canadian goods such as knitted sweaters and honey. Economists and business leaders have warned that sweeping tariffs raise prices for consumers.

Carney said he suspended negotiations after Washington introduced last-minute proposals that were “unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of the deal.” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued that Canada disrupted progress on the deal and was “continuing to maintain its prolonged retaliation against the United States.”

Canada will impose retaliatory tariffs beginning Sept. 8, the details of which have yet to be revealed.

“You’re at war when you’re attacked,” Carney told reporters Saturday. “We were attacked.”

Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, obtained its name from the Huron word Ontarí’io, which means “great lake” or “beautiful water.”

The body of water serves as a key shipping route that connects the rest of the Great Lakes and the Atlantic Ocean via major port cities like Toronto and Rochester, New York. 

The potential name change is just the latest example of Trump clashing with allies since his return to office, oftentimes arguing that foreign governments are conducting unfair economic practices as justification for his aggressive tariff policy. 

He’s also pursued symbolic name changes as a show of force.

Trump signed an executive order on his first day of office to rename the Gulf of Mexico, which borders the U.S., Mexico and Cuba, the “Gulf of America.” The action resulted in a frantic rollout process under administration pressure. The abrupt change also vexed Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, whose administration sued Google for changing the name on its mapping software.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez

entries.title: Judge Dismisses Ghislaine Maxwell’s ‘Frivolous’ Attempt to Toss Convictions
entries.summary: The opinion says the longtime Jeffrey Epstein accomplice had raised “outright falsehoods” in her “lengthy and rambling” petition.
entries.content:
A federal judge forcefully rejected Ghislaine Maxwell’s attempt to vacate her conviction and sentence for helping Jeffrey Epstein sexually abuse underage girls, ruling Tuesday that her claims of constitutional violations were “frivolous.”

U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer in New York wrote in an opinion that nothing in Maxwell’s "lengthy and rambling” petition — filed in December without assistance from lawyers — offered support to reconsider her five felony convictions or 20-year federal prison sentence.

“Her petition’s claims are demonstrably meritless, and generally based on speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods,” Engelmayer wrote. “There is no fact that Maxwell fairly puts in dispute that has any potential to disturb the outcome of her trial.”

Maxwell, Epstein’s longtime accomplice and former romantic partner, was convicted in 2021 of helping Epstein groom, traffic and coerce minors into sex with the late sex offender and well-connected financier. Epstein died in federal custody in 2019 while facing federal sex-trafficking charges in what was ruled a suicide.

Maxwell was initially imprisoned in a federal detention center in Florida, but the Justice Department last year transferred Maxwell to a minimum-security prison camp in Texas known for its lax conditions. The move came shortly after Todd Blanche, then the deputy attorney general, interviewed Maxwell in Tallahassee amid uproar over the Justice Department’s handling of files in the Epstein case.

Maxwell had sought a new trial and appealed her sentence and conviction without success. The Supreme Court declined to take up her case last year.

Maxwell’s latest petition contained dozens of claims about what she said were errors and violations of her rights surrounding her trial in New York in 2021 and subsequent sentencing — none of which the judge found convincing.

In his bluntly-worded 67-page ruling, Engelmayer said Maxwell repeatedly misinterpreted legal issues, tacked irrelevant exhibits onto her filings and raised baseless arguments about how prosecutors handled her case. She also missed deadlines and raised claims that were barred under court procedure.

In one claim, Maxwell argued she was selectively prosecuted, saying the Justice Department could have charged alleged co-conspirators or other men who entered into settlements with Epstein’s victims. The judge said that was “patently frivolous.”

“Maxwell served for years as Epstein’s indispensable recruiter and groomer in chief. She does not point to any other person who abetted Epstein in this manner or to this degree,” he wrote. “On the contrary, Maxwell has not implicated any other person in the child sex abuse scheme.”

She also argued that documents in the trove of Epstein files released by the Justice Department showed that prosecutors had failed to turn over evidence that could have helped prove her innocence.

The judge disagreed, saying that, if anything, the materials showed that the prosecution team “went above and beyond its disclosure obligations.”

Another of Maxwell’s claims accused prosecutors of improperly colluding with victims’ attorneys and manipulating them into bringing the charges against her.

The judge said prosecutors had acted appropriately in meeting with victims and their counsel.

“Prosecutors’ conferral with and receipt of information from witnesses, victims, and other private actors — directly or through their counsel — is commonplace in the building of a criminal case and the preparation for a criminal trial,” the judge wrote. “It does not transform such persons into members of the prosecution team.”

The judge noted that many of Maxwell’s claims had already been rejected by previous judges, and that she failed to raise others earlier in the proceedings. He denied her request for an evidentiary hearing on her arguments.

A Maxwell attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
entries.author: Derek Hawkins

entries.title: Mike Lindell Withholds Payment for Minnesota Election Recount
entries.summary: The bedding magnate, who has refused to concede his loss in the Republican primary for governor, said his team found “anomalies” that extend to all candidates.
entries.content:
MyPillow founder Mike Lindell is withholding payment for a recount — that he requested — after he lost the Republican primary for Minnesota governor this month, his campaign said in a news release Monday.

Lindell, a bedding magnate who rose to prominence as one of the highest-profile boosters of President Donald Trump’s unfounded claims of widespread election fraud in the 2020 election, said he backed off wiring nearly $1 million to state officials because of the recount rules laid out by the secretary of state’s office.

Lindell alleges that Steve Simon, Minnesota’s top election official, narrowed the recount’s scope: Instead of reexamining all ballots, the recount would only cover those cast for Lindell and the winner of the primary, Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth, and not for the other five Republican gubernatorial candidates.

The decision incensed Lindell, who alleged his team had found "anomalies" that applied “to all of the candidates, not simply Lindell and Demuth.”

His campaign vowed to take legal action over the discrepancy.
https://x.com/realMikeLindell/status/2092021511326765249?s=20Lindell remains an ardent believer in widely debunked claims of voter fraud. He has endured social media bans and legal trouble over his activism, including a $1.3 billion defamation lawsuit from Dominion Voting Systems, now known as Liberty Vote.

But at least one high-profile backer is still embracing Lindell: Trump, who endorsed the Minnesota businessman’s gubernatorial bid last month, saying, “Nobody has sacrificed more than Mike Lindell in fighting for our country, especially when it comes to Election Integrity.”

Lindell has refused to concede to Demuth since the Aug. 11 election. He released a statement a week later that he would privately fund a recount and audit of “every paper ballot cast in the Aug. 11, 2026 Republican primary election for Governor of Minnesota.” Lindell claimed his team identified “vote totals that moved backwards during the reporting,” “counties reporting more votes than cast” and “unusual synchronized vote totals across all seven Republican candidates” — which he alleges are signs of tampering with the results that could sway the vote in his favor.

Lindell’s campaign said Monday that under the recount rules laid out by state officials, Democratic ballots would not be recounted, “even though the same ballot form was used for both gubernatorial primaries.” The actions, his campaign added, put Lindell in an “untenable position.”

If he were to submit the $825,000 fee under the new scope, the recount would “not be conducted in a lawful manner nor would it address the election anomalies cited by his team,” the Monday press release said. And if Lindell fought for a wider scope, he would not meet a payment deadline “for the unlawful recount.”

The Minnesota secretary of state’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Lindell’s voter fraud claims or his decision to withhold payment. Simon has previously pushed back against federal inquiries into the state’s election system, saying “Minnesota’s elections are fair, accurate, honest, and secure.”

Demuth will face Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who won the Democratic nomination by a wide margin, in November.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez

entries.title: Secret Service Investigating $10M Bounty Iran Placed on Barron Trump
entries.summary: A spokesperson said the agency looks into “anything that can be perceived as a threat.”
entries.content:
The U.S. Secret Service is looking into a video, aired on Iranian state media, that suggests the country has placed a bounty on Barron Trump.

It’s a threat that comes as hostilities between the two countries spiral after the collapse of a ceasefire deal earlier this month.

The video, broadcast last weekend by state media outlet IRIB, opened with a banner stating: “Where to kill Barron Trump?!” The video then goes on to list a number of places it says the president’s youngest son frequents, including Trump Tower in New York City.

It ends with a narrator saying people were “eagerly waiting” to receive a $10 million reward for his assassination, CNN reported.

The video is apparently part of a series. A similar video emerged last month targeting first lady Melania Trump.

“The US Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees,” Secret Service spokesperson Nate Herring said in a statement Tuesday. “Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence.”

Iranian media has aired multiple threats toward President Donald Trump and his family since the U.S. launched a major attack that killed the country’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in February.

An Iranian threat last month prompted the president to take a secret flight out of Turkey after sneaking off Air Force One in a catering truck.

Trump acknowledged the threats last month in an interview with the New York Post, adding that he’s told aides and military leaders to launch a massive offensive against Iran if they were to succeed in assassinating him.

“I’ve been on their list for a long time,” he said. “I’ve left instructions, if anything happens, to just literally bomb them at levels that they’ve never seen before.”
